html:
The Kinsey Reports were two large studies of American sexual behaviour by the zoologist Alfred Kinsey and his team: Sexual Behavior in the Human Male in 1948 and Sexual Behavior in the Human Female in 1953.

They were built on thousands of private interviews, about 5,300 men and 5,900 women, collected at Indiana University by the Institute for Sex Research. The male volume was a thick, dry book of tables, yet it became a bestseller. It reported that acts then widely condemned or illegal, from sex before marriage to same-sex contact, were far more common than people said. Kinsey also proposed a scale from 0 to 6 of sexual orientation, rejecting a simple split into two kinds of people.

The books caused a storm. Churches and politicians attacked them, and statisticians attacked the sampling, which leaned on volunteers, prisoners and certain groups. In 1954 the Rockefeller Foundation ended its funding under political pressure, in the Cold War climate of the 1950s.

The reports began open public talk of sex in the United States and are seen as a step toward the sexual revolution of the 1960s.
